Flexible definitions of "primary residence" and "second home"

Your home can be your "primary residence" even if you don't live in it 365 days a year - and even if you sometimes earn a little income from it. The IRS allows you to rent your home for up to 14 days without it becoming a rental property.
Your motor home or boat could be a "second home"

The IRS says that as long as a place is "livable," it can be a home; and they define "livable" as having a working bathroom and kitchen. In addition, you must spend at least 15 nights a year in your boat or RV. Check with a tax professional; the interest on the loan may be tax-deductible, like it is for your primary residence. Keep in mind, however, that if you claim your boat or RV as a second home, you can't also buy a second house and deduct the interest on that loan, too.
Is it a "vacation home" or a "rental property ?"

If you rent a home for most of the year, but sometimes use it yourself, it may be a "vacation home." To be a "vacation home," you can use it for up to 10% of the days it's rented out per year; or up to 14 days per year; whichever is greater. For example, if you rent a home for 320 days a year, you can use it yourself for up to 32 days that year and still call it a "vacation home." A "rental property" is one you own primarily for investment purposes. In other words, it's rented for too many days during the year to qualify it as either a second home or vacation home.
Has a front or back yard, one mailing address, and only your family lives there.
Same as single family detached, except it physically shares a wall with a neighbor's home.
An apartment unit that you own.
Sometimes called a "pre-fab" home; it's "live-in-ready" when delivered to you.

How to Decide If Refinancing Is Right for You
When interest rates are low, refinancing may allow you to replace your current mortgage with a new loan with more advantageous terms. Here are some of the potential benefits of refinancing.

Refinancing into a mortgage with a lower interest rate translates to lower monthly payments, freeing up extra cash in your budget that can be put towards other goals such as saving for college, retirement savings, paying down other debts, etc.

Lower interest rates may make it possible to switch to a shorter-term mortgage — say from a 30-year loan to a 15-year loan — enabling you to build equity in your home faster and pay less interest over the life of the loan.

verifyText.value: The monthly savings from refinancing a mortgage can be significant, but they're not the full story. Before deciding to refinance, it's important to run the numbers to see if the financial benefits outweigh the costs. Two critical metrics to consider are the break-even point and total loan cost.

The break-even point is the point at which the monthly savings created by a mortgage refinance offsets the upfront cost of refinancing. For example, if you're paying $4,500 in closing costs and you're saving $250 a month on your mortgage, it'll take you 18 months to reach the break-even point. Your breakeven point isn't quite as critical if you plan on staying in your home for a long time. However, if you plan to sell your home and move before reaching your break-even point, you'll have lost money by refinancing instead of saving it.

Your breakeven point will tell you when you'll start saving money on a monthly basis, but it doesn't tell you how much your loan will cost over the long run or whether it'll make it cheaper to own your home. To do that, you'll need to compare the total cost of your current mortgage with the new one. Of course, the cheapest total cost isn't always the best choice for a particular homeowner. Whether the additional long-term cost of an extended loan term is worth it is a personal financial decision that involves many other factors unique to you.

Your FICO score (an acronym for the credit scoring service, Fair Isaacs Company) is an assigned number between 300 and 850 that indicates to lenders your capacity to repay a loan. It can change regularly, as new information is sent by your creditors to one or more of the three major national credit bureaus, Experian, Trans Union, and Equifax. The higher your FICO score, the more likely you will qualify for a mortgage loan and the best interest rates.
A FICO score is comprised of 5 parts:

Your types of accounts and your payment record; any bankruptcies, legal judgments, wage garnishments, etc.; the severity and amount of late payments; the number of past-due items and when they occurred. (35%)
How much you currently owe and on what types of accounts; number of accounts with balances; the proportion of credit lines still available. (30%)
Time since accounts opened; by specific type of account; since last activity. (15%)
Number of recently opened accounts, by type and date opened; recent credit inquiries and date of inquiries; reestablishment of good credit after payment delinquencies. (10%)
The number and types of credit accounts available for your use. (10%)
By federal law, you're entitled to a free credit report once every 12 months from each of the three major credit bureaus - Experian, TransUnion, or Equifax.
